Noun ( UK ) A male dancer dressed as a horse who cavorts through the town pretending to capture young maidens, as part of a May Day festival in Padstow, Cornwall, England. From hobby horse , with h -dropping characteristic of West Country English. Compare hoss .
Noun Pronunciation spelling of holiday . A representation of the pronunciation of holiday by a speaker whose dialect lacks the voiceless glottal fricative or transition ([h]).
/tɪz/ Contraction (literary or archaic, also occasionally informal) Contraction of it +‎ is . Synonym: it's

/ˈeɪ.ʃəs/ Suffix Of, relating to, resembling or containing the thing suffixed Belonging to a taxonomic family or other group Suffixal construction from (1) Latin ‑āceus (“belonging to, of the nature of”) +‎ -ous , from oblique stem of -āx, -ācis +‎ -eus and (2) -acea +‎ -ous . Also variant of -acious .
Suffix Forms names of hearing impairments. From Ancient Greek ἄκουσις (ákousis, “hearing”).

Suffix ( Internet slang ) Forms nouns which refer to acts of manipulation which seek to elicit a particular response. From bait .
Suffix Synonym of -borough . From boro , from Old English burh (“fortified place”).

/ˈsɛntrɪk/ Suffix Having a specified number of centres. Having a specified object at the centre, or as the focus of attention. Representing a combining form of Ancient Greek κεντρικός (kentrikós, “central”). Cognate with Bengali -কেন্দ্রিক (-kendrik)
/-ˈkɑkəs/, /-ˈkɒkəs/ Suffix any spherical microorganism From New Latin coccus , from Latin coccum , from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”).

Suffix An empty suffix, perhaps derived from the past-tense suffix above, added in some dialects to the present tense forms of some words which then add an additional -ed in the past tense. Marks ordinals written in digits when the final term of the spelled number is "second" or "third"
/dɪl.ɒl/, /dɪl.ɔl/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of vasodilators. From -dil- (“vasodilator”) +‎ -olol (“β-adrenoceptor antagonist”).
Suffix Forms nouns related to flowers. Borrowed from Latin -flōrus (adapted through -ous ).
Suffix language ( anatomy ) tongue From Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă, “tongue; language”).
Suffix ( geometry ) Forms the names of solid figures bounded by a certain number of planes (polyhedra). From Ancient Greek ἕδρα (hédra, “face of a geometrical solid”).
Suffix Used to form adjectives from nouns or from other adjectives, with the meaning "of or pertaining to" the preceding component. From -ist +‎ -ic .

/-əˈzeɪ.ʃən/, /-ˌaɪˈzeɪ.ʃən/ Suffix Forms nouns denoting the act, process, or result of doing/making what is denoted by the noun/adjective. Usage Note See the usage notes on -ize . /lɛkt/ Suffix ( linguistics ) A (language) variety. From the terminal element of dialect , thus representing the Ancient Greek element -λεκτος (-lektos), ultimately from λέγω (légō, “I say or speak”).

/ˌlɑɡ/, /ˌlɔɡ/ Suffix US standard spelling of -logue .
Suffix Denotes maximum dimensions of a vessel that can travel through the given canal. Clipping of maximum . Clipping of maximize .
/nət.ənt/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of neurokinin NK 3 receptor antagonists. From ne(uro)- +‎ -tant (“neurokinin receptor antagonist”).

Suffix Used to form the names of several commercial companies and products. ( entertainment industry ) Used to form pejorative terms associated with commercial bribery. Used to form humorous and pejorative words. Used to form words relating to oil or oiliness From Latin -ola , -ula , feminine form of -ulus , -lus (diminutive suffix). From Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”).

/ˈɑləd͡ʒi/, /ˈɒləd͡ʒi/ Suffix ( often humorous ) added to an ordinary English word to create a name for a (possibly non-existent) field of study. Suffix Eye From Ancient Greek ὠπός (ōpós), genitive of ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”).
Suffix Forms names of speech disorders. From Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “speech”).
Suffix Forms names of systems of agriculture. From geoponics (“agriculture”), which is ultimately from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-, “earth”) +‎ πόνος (pónos, “work, toil”) +‎ -ικός (-ikós).

Suffix Added to a noun to form an adjective denoting imperviousness to that noun. Added to a noun to form a verb denoting a process to make something impervious to that noun. Usage Note Often used as the second part of a combined form (such as bullet-proof) rather than as a true suffix (as in waterproof) From the adjective proof (“fully resistant”), from the same Old French root as prove .
/ɹiə/, /ɹɪə/ Suffix ( American spelling ) flowing. From Ancient Greek ῥοία (rhoía, “flow, flux”).
/ˈsɛlvz/, /ˈsɛlz/ Suffix Used in forming intensive and reflexive forms of the plural personal pronouns. Usage Note See usage notes at -self.
Suffix Used in the names of software houses. From software .
Suffix ( furry fandom ) Added to a noun to describe a taur with the lower body of the noun's form. Clipping of centaur or from compounding of taur .
/tɹɪ.d͡ʒiːn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of sodium channel blockers used as signal transduction modulators. Probably from tr(ansduction +‎ (s)ig(nal) +‎ -ine .

/-ˈtɹoʊˌpɪzəm/, /-ˈtɹəʊpɪz(ə)m/ Suffix ( sciences ) movement, turning. ( biology ) growth towards. From Latin tropus (English trope ) +‎ -ism , from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a turn, way, manner, style, a trope or figure of speech, a mode in music, a mode or mood in logic”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”). Early use in botany as geotropism and heliotropism .
Suffix Having one or more valences. Back-formation from valence .

Noun ( computing ) An overlay file. From the extension for an overlay file. A file used in memory limited systems to overwrite portions of program execution space (code and data) to enable other operations; such as found in 8-/10-/12-/16-bit systems. Abbreviation of overlay .

Noun ( automotive ) A performance measure for automobiles that measures elapsed time; the time taken for an automobile that starts from a standing start to accelerate to 60 miles per hour (roughly 100 km/h). From 0 +‎ 60 .

Proper Noun The fictional MI6 agent James Bond. Noun A special agent resembling the fictional James Bond in capability, charisma, etc. (soccer, slang) A term for an attacking player in football (soccer) who fails to score a goal or an assist in their first seven match appearances. Often used to insinuate poor or underwhelming performance. From James Bond's code number in the series of books by Ian Fleming.
Noun Initialism of zero gravity . Initialism of zero gauge .

Proper Noun Abbreviation of 1 Corinthians .

Noun ( organic chemistry ) MPP+, the active metabolite of MPTP. ( neurotoxicology ) A neurotoxin that cannot cross the blood-brain barrier but which, once in contact, can destroy the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra.

/wɒn ʌp/, /ˈwʌn ʌp/ Noun ( video games ) An item that grants the player an extra life in the game, staving off game over by one more try. ( video games ) In a game with multiple players, an indicator or identifier of player 1. "Extra life" sense borrowed from Japanese 1UP ( ワンアップ ) ( wan'appu ) and perhaps popularized by Super Mario Bros. (1985); but the term existed earlier in multi-player pinball and other arcade games in the 1960s, where "1Up" and "2Up" were used as flashing notifications to ...
Noun A flood event that has a 1% probability of occurring in any given year; an exceptionally large flood.

/tɛnˈeɪ.ti/ Noun An aerial maneuver in which the performer spins through three full revolutions. ( informal ) Sodium fluoroacetate poison. From 1080° of rotation angle. From its original catalogue number.

Noun ( geometry ) Synonym of icosagon : A polygon with twenty sides and twenty angles. From 20 +‎ -gon .

Noun (US, slang) A ho, a sexually promiscuous woman, a prostitute. Usage Note Often used online to circumvent automated filters. The number 304 , when displayed on a seven-segment display (e.g. of a calculator), resembles "hOE" when viewed upside down. See also calculator spelling.

Verb (Philippines, slang) cheated; scammed 349 +‎ -ed . 349 was the number of the jackpot printed on 800-thousand bottlecaps in the Pepsi Number Fever. Pepsi Cola refused to honor the jackpot, leading to nationwide riots.

From 3 (“three”) +‎ X (“cross, by, against”) +‎ 3 +‎ basketball . From being a form of basketball with three players facing three players on the two sides.
/ˌfɔɹ.oʊˈfɔɹ.peɪdʒ/ Noun ( Internet ) The result of trying to follow a broken link within a website. From 404 (error message) +‎ page (“webpage”).
